entries.title: Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai: a survey from before the eruption
paragraphs: Important: the terrain in this mission predates the 15 January 2022 eruption. This tile is built from bathymetry gathered before that date (surveys including a November 2015 WASSP multibeam survey and further multibeam work in September 2017), and it shows the volcano as it stood then, not as it stands now. Nothing in this game recreates the post-eruption seafloor -- see below for what the real surveys found instead.

Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai is a submarine volcano in the Tonga archipelago, the summit of a roughly 2-km-high edifice rising from the surrounding seafloor. Before 2022, its caldera -- a broad volcanic basin about 4.5 km across -- sat around 150 m below sea level, and two small islands, Hunga Tonga and Hunga Ha'apai, poked above the water on its rim, joined by a shallow saddle.

On 15 January 2022, the volcano produced one of the most powerful eruptions ever recorded by modern instruments: an eruption column that reached roughly 58 km into the atmosphere, an atmospheric pressure shockwave that circled the globe several times, and a tsunami that struck Tonga and was recorded across the Pacific. Locally, waves reached as high as 15-22 m on some islands; the eruption and tsunami killed at least 6 people in Tonga (plus further reported deaths and injuries) and caused widespread damage.

The eruption triggered a catastrophic collapse of the summit caldera. Surveys by the NIWA-Nippon Foundation Tonga Eruption Seabed Mapping Project (TESMaP), beginning within months of the eruption, found the caldera floor had dropped from about 150 m to roughly 850 m deep, and widened from about 4.5 km to about 4.8 km across. The two islands are now smaller and no longer connected. None of that post-eruption terrain is shown in this mission; this tile is the 'before' picture only.

facts.label: Edifice height
facts.value: ~2 km from seafloor to the islands

entries.title: The caldera floor, before 2022
paragraphs: This broad, gently sloping basin was the floor of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai's summit caldera before the 2022 eruption, roughly 150 m below the surface. This tile's own terrain reads about 132 m deep here, close to that published figure.

Multibeam surveys carried out in 2015 (WASSP, aboard the vessel Pacific Rose) and again in 2017 mapped this floor and the caldera walls around it, providing the last detailed picture of the volcano before its catastrophic collapse.
The caldera you are scanning collapsed to roughly 850 m deep in January 2022; what you see here no longer exists in this form.

facts.label: Pre-eruption survey
facts.value: WASSP multibeam, Nov 2015; further multibeam, Sep 2017

entries.title: The islands, joined
paragraphs: Before 2022, the volcano's two subaerial peaks, Hunga Tonga and Hunga Ha'apai, were joined by a shallow saddle of rock and reef just above sea level, visible here at the surface. Together they formed the only visible part of the roughly 2-km-tall volcanic edifice beneath them.

The 15 January 2022 eruption changed this permanently: NIWA's post-eruption survey found the islands 'smaller and no longer joined together.' A large part of the saddle, and much of the original island material, was blasted away or collapsed into the sea during the eruption.
This tile shows only the earlier, connected state, from before the eruption. No post-eruption island shape is modelled here.

facts.label: State shown here
facts.value: pre-2022: islands joined by a shallow saddle

sources.title: Ongoing Activity at Hunga Submarine Volcano, Tonga — Walker et al. 2024, AGU

entries.title: The inner caldera wall
paragraphs: Descending from the shallow caldera floor, the terrain steepens into the caldera's inner wall -- part of the crater rim that, before 2022, enclosed the summit basin. This tile reads roughly 469 m deep along this stretch of slope.

No source consulted names this exact point specifically; it is picked out from this tile's own pre-eruption bathymetry as a representative section of the caldera wall, rather than a feature with its own published survey description. Treat the depth as a real reading from this tile, and the description of it as a 'caldera wall' as an interpretation of the surrounding terrain.

sources.title: Global Multi-Resolution Topography (GMRT) Synthesis — Ryan et al. 2009, doi:10.1029/2008GC002332
Ongoing Activity at Hunga Submarine Volcano, Tonga — Walker et al. 2024, AGU

entries.title: The outer flank of a 2-km volcano
paragraphs: Beyond the caldera rim, the seafloor drops away down the outer flank of the wider volcanic edifice -- this tile reads roughly 1,029 m deep here. The whole structure, from this outer base to the summit islands, rises about 2 km from the surrounding seafloor, making Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai one of the larger submarine volcanoes in the Tonga-Kermadec arc.

This part of the seafloor lies outside the caldera itself and was not directly involved in the 2022 collapse, which was confined to the summit basin. It is shown here as real, if pre-eruption, survey terrain.
